question_text: The framework of the external nose:
option_b: Upper ½ is bony, and lower 1/2 is cartilaginous
option_c: The upper 2/3rd is bony and the lower 1/3rd is cartilaginous
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The external nose is formed by both bone and cartilage.
  • The upper one-third of the structure is bony, while the lower two-thirds are cartilaginous.

External nose anatomy:

  • Shaped like a pyramid, with its root directed upward and the base downward.
  • The framework is osteocartilaginous and covered by skin and small muscles.
  • Bony part → nasal bones, frontal bone, and the ascending process of the maxilla.
  • Cartilaginous part → includes upper lateral cartilage, lower lateral (alar) cartilages, sesamoid cartilages, and septal cartilage.
    • Upper lateral cartilages: extend downward from the nasal bones and join the septal cartilage; their lower edge forms the nasal valve (limen nasi).
    • Lower lateral (alar) cartilages: U-shaped with a lateral crus forming the ala and a medial crus forming the columella; they overlap the lower border of the upper lateral cartilages.
    • Lesser alar (sesamoid) cartilages: small accessory cartilages situated above the alar cartilage.
    • Septal cartilage (quadrangular cartilage): supports the cartilaginous dorsum; damage or resection may cause a supratip depression.

Explanation of other options:

  • Option B & C: Misrepresent the relative proportions of bony and cartilaginous parts.
  • Option D: Incorrect since the framework is well-defined as 1/3 bony and 2/3 cartilaginous.

question_text: While going up for a rebound, a basketball player jams her middle finger against the ball. She experiences severe pain and the trainer notes that she can no longer extend the distal phalanx of the finger. The injury has avulsed (torn away from the bone) which structure from her distal phalanx to produce this condition?
explanation:
The extensor expansions are the expanded distal ends of the extensor tendons which wrap around the heads of the metacarpals and the bases of the proximal phalanges and insert on the bases of the middle and distal phalanges. These extensor expansions hold the extensor tendon in the middle of the digit and provide a place for the lumbricals and interossei to attach. If an extensor expansion was torn, the extensor tendon would not be held in place and a lumbrical would be torn from its attachment. This would impair extension at the joint.

Extensor carpi radialis brevis and longus are involved with extending the wrist and abducting the hand. These muscles do not produce extension at the fingers. Extensor digiti minimi and extensor indicis help with extension at the 5th and 2nd finger, but they do not act at the third finger.

question_text: A student is rollerblading on the road and while trying to avoid a bicyclist falls heavily on his right wrist. After the fall he notes severe pain in the anatomical snuff box. Radiological studies reveal a fracture of the bone deep to the snuff box called the

question_text: All of the following are supernumerary bones, except;

Explanation:

Accessory (Supernumerary) Bones:

  • Presence: Not always present; occur as ununited epiphyses from extra centers of ossification.

Sutural bones (Option C):

  • Extra bones formed within the cranial sutures, especially lambdoid.
  • Due to additional ossification centres.
  • Well-established type of supernumerary bone.

Key takeaways:

Rider's bone is heterotopic bone. It develops in adductor longus muscle in horse riders.

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding the layer of bone involved?
option_b: Progenitor cells are present in the outer fibrous layer
option_c: It is continuous with the capsule of the joint
option_d: It is devoid of nerve supply
explanation:
The given X-ray shows Codman's triangle, which is due to an irregular periosteal reaction (outermost layer), commonly seen in patients with osteosarcoma. The periosteum is a thick fibrous membrane that covers the outer surface of all bones, except at the joint surfaces and insertion points of tendons and ligaments (entheses). At the articular margin, the periosteum is continuous with the capsule of the joint.

The periosteum has 2 layers:

  • The outer fibrous layer - contains fibroblasts.
  • The inner cambium layer (osteogenic layer) - contains progenitor cells that develop into osteoblasts.

Periosteum gets nourishment from periosteal arteries. It has a rich nerve supply, which makes it the most sensitive part of the bone.

Joints in the body are structurally classified into three main types:

  • Fibrous joints

  • Cartilaginous joints
    • Bones are united by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage.
      • Examples: synchondrosis, symphysis.
  • Synovial joints
    • Possess a joint cavity, articular cartilage, and a fibrous capsule.
    • Most mobile category of joints.
    • Classified based on the shape of articular surfaces.

question_text: Identify the type of joint marked in the given image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The joint marked in the given image is inferior tibiofibular joint. It is a syndesmosis uniting the lower ends of the tibia and the fibula.

The bony surfaces are connected by a very strong interosseous ligament, which forms the chief bond of union between the lower ends of these bones. The joints can be classified based upon the type of connective tissue and presence of absence of a joint cavity into three types :

  • Fibrous: the bones forming the joints are united by fibrous connective tissue. It is of 3 types :
    • Sutures: bones are connected by sutural ligaments. e.g. sutures in skull.
    • Syndesmosis: bones are connected by greater amount of connective tissues. e.g. interosseous radioulnar joint, interosseous tibiofibular joint, inferior tibiofibular joint
    • Gomphosis: specialized fibrous joint restricted to fixation of teeth in alveolar socket.
  • Cartilaginous: Bones forming the joints are united by hyaline or fibrocartilage. It is of 2 types
    • Primary: bones connected by hyaline cartilage. e.g. 1st chondrosternal joint etc
    • Secondary: articular surface covered by hyaline cartilage that is connected by fibrocartilage. e.g. pubic symphysis, Intervertebral disc , Manubriosternal etc.
  • Synovial: These joints posses a cavity and the articular ends of bones forming the joint are enclosed in fibrous capsule.

Types of synovial joints:

Explanation for the other options:

  • Saddle joints (e.g., carpometacarpal joint of the thumb) are synovial.
  • Plane joints (e.g., intercarpal joints) are synovial.
  • Primary cartilaginous joints (synchondrosis) use hyaline cartilage (e.g., epiphyseal plates).

Key Takeaways:

The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous joint known as a syndesmosis.

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding long bones?
option_a: Cancellous bone is absent in the epiphysis
option_b: Cancellous bone is present in the outer cortex
option_c: Haversian system is absent in cancellous bone
option_d: Compact bone has lamellae arranged in a meshwork
explanation:
The Haversian system is seen in compact bones, not cancellous bones.

Based on their macroscopic structure, bones can be classified as compact and cancellous (spongy) bones.

Compact bones are composed of cylindrical structural units called Haversian systems or osteons. Each Haversian system contains a central canal within which the small blood vessels, nerves, and endosteum are present.

This canal is surrounded by multiple layers or lamellae of the calcified matrix containing type I collagen fibers. These canals communicate with each other by Volkmann's canal.

The lamellae of the cancellous/spongy bone are arranged in a meshwork, and hence do not form Haversian systems.

The diaphysis and outer cortex of long bones are predominantly made of compact bone, while the epiphysis and inner medulla are predominantly made of cancellous bone.

question_text: Which of the following types of joints is not associated with this bone?
explanation:
Explanation:

The vertebra participates in various joint types, but it is not associated with synchondrosis.

  • Synchondrosis is a primary cartilaginous joint where bones are united by hyaline cartilage.
  • These joints are usually temporary, typically found in the developing skeleton, such as:
    • Epiphyseal growth plates of long bones in children
    • The first sternocostal joint (between the first rib and the sternum)

These joints are not present in the vertebral column.

Explanation of other options:

Syndesmosis (Option A): A syndesmosis is a type of fibrous joint in which bones are joined by ligaments or an interosseous membrane. In the vertebral column, examples of syndesmosis include the ligamentum flavum and the interspinous ligaments, which connect adjacent vertebrae. Therefore, syndesmosis is a joint type that is clearly associated with vertebrae.

Plane Synovial Joint (Option C): Plane synovial joints are characterized by flat or slightly curved articular surfaces that allow for gliding movements. The facet joints (zygapophyseal joints) between the superior and inferior articular processes of adjacent vertebrae are examples of plane synovial joints. Consequently, this type of joint is present in the vertebral column.

question_text: Which of the following is not an end artery?
explanation:
Explanation:

The arteries supplying the diaphysis of long bones are not end arteries. These regions receive blood from multiple sources, primarily the nutrient artery, periosteal arteries, and metaphyseal vessels. Because of this rich anastomotic network, occlusion of one vessel does not usually lead to infarction, making them non-end arteries.

End Arteries:

  • Definition:End arteries are arteries that do not anastomose with their neighbouring arteries, meaning they have no alternative blood supply.
  • Examples:
  • Central artery of the retina
  • Labyrinthine artery of the internal ear
  • Central branches of cerebral arteries
  • Vasa recta of mesenteric arteries
  • Arteries of the spleen, kidney, lungs, and metaphysis of long bones
  • Clinical Significance:Occlusion of an end artery can lead to serious nutritional disturbances and tissue death. For example, occlusion of the central artery of the retina can result in blindness.

Key takeaways:

End arteries are arteries that do not anastomose with neighboring arteries, and their occlusion can lead to serious tissue damage, such as blindness from the central artery of the retina.

question_text: A 12-year-old child presents for evaluation of growth plate injuries after a minor fall. Which type of joint connects the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone, and is primarily responsible for longitudinal bone growth?
explanation:
Explanation:

A synchondrosis is a primary cartilaginous joint where the epiphysis and diaphysis are separated by hyaline cartilage, known as the growth plate (physis).

  • Function: Allows longitudinal growth of long bones during childhood and adolescence.
  • Clinical Relevance: Injury to the growth plate can result in growth disturbances or limb length discrepancies.
  • Examples: Epiphyseal plates of long bones; the joint between the first rib and manubrium is a permanent synchondrosis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Symphysis (Option A): A secondary cartilaginous joint where bones are connected by fibrocartilage, allowing slight movement (e.g., pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs). These are permanent joints, not involved in longitudinal growth.

Synostosis (Option C): Refers to fusion of bones, where cartilage is entirely replaced by bone; occurs after growth completion. Does not allow movement or growth.

Syndesmosis (Option D): A fibrous joint where bones are connected by a ligament or interosseous membrane (e.g., distal tibiofibular joint), allowing limited movement. Not involved in bone growth.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • High-Yield Points:
    • Synchondrosis: Primary cartilaginous, hyaline cartilage, temporary, allows longitudinal growth.
    • Symphysis: Secondary cartilaginous, fibrocartilage, slightly mobile, permanent.
    • Synostosis: Bone fusion, immobile, post-growth.
    • Syndesmosis: Fibrous joint, ligament/interosseous membrane, limited movement.

Clinical Correlation:

  • Epiphyseal fractures (Salter-Harris classification) occur at synchondroses.
  • Mismanagement can lead to limb length discrepancies.
  • Knowledge of joint type helps in orthopedic surgery and pediatric trauma.

question_text: The coracoid process of scapula is an example of which of the following type of the epiphysis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The coracoid process of the scapula is an example of an atavistic epiphysis. This type of epiphysis represents a phylogenetic remnant of a bone that existed separately in lower vertebrates. In humans, this ancestral bone becomes fused to the scapula during development, thus forming an atavistic epiphysis. Its evolutionary origin differentiates it from pressure, traction, or aberrant epiphyses.

Epiphysis:

  • The ends and tips of a bone which ossify from secondary centres are called epiphyses.
  • These are of the following types.
  • Pressure epiphysis (Option A): It is articular and takes part in transmission of the weight. Examples: head of femur; lower end of radius, etc.
  • Traction epiphysis (Option B): It is non-articular and does not take part in the transmission of the weight. It always provides attachment to one or more tendons which exert a traction on the epiphysis. It ossifies later than the pressure epiphyses.
  • Examples: trochanters of femur and tubercles of humerus
  • Atavistic epiphysis: It is phylogenetically an independent bone which in man becomes fused to another bone.
  • Examples: coracoid process of scapula and os trigonum or lateral tubercle of talus.
  • Aberrant epiphysis (Option D): It is not always present.
  • Examples: epiphysis at the head of the first metacarpal and at the base of other metacarpal bones.

Key takeaways:

The epiphysis refers to the ends of a bone that ossify from secondary centers, with types including pressure, traction, atavistic, and aberrant epiphyses.

question_text: Nutrient artery runs ?

The epiphyseal plate (growth plate) is a hyaline cartilage layer that separates the epiphysis from the metaphysis. It receives nourishment from both the epiphyseal and metaphyseal arteries. Fractures involving epiphyseal plates are known as Salter-Harris fractures.

The growing ends of bones include:

  • Upper limb: Upper end of humerus, and lower ends of radius and ulna
  • Lower limb: Lower end of femur, and upper end of tibia

question_text: 'The secondary ossification center that appears first, fuses last'. Which of the following bones violates this law?

question_text: The largest ball and socket joint in the body?
explanation:
Your hip joint is one of the largest joints in your body. The top of your thigh bone (femur head) that fits into your hip bone (pelvis) is approximately 48 millimeters to 55 millimeters in diameter on the average person. This is about the same size as a small apple.

The socket area (acetabulum) is inside the pelvis. The ball part of this joint is the top of the thighbone (femur). It joins with the acetabulum to form the hip joint. The hip is one of the most stable joints in the body.

question_text: All of the followings are examples of primary cartilaginous joint, except;
explanation:
Explanation:

Costovertebral joints are synovial plane joints, not primary cartilaginous joints. They involve articulation between the head of the rib and the bodies of thoracic vertebrae, containing a synovial cavity and allowing gliding movements during respiration. Because they include a joint capsule and synovial membrane, they do not belong to the primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis) category.

Spheno-occipital joint (Option A): The spheno-occipital joint is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) where bones are united by hyaline cartilage. It allows growth during development and later ossifies. This type of joint fits the definition of a primary cartilaginous joint.

First chondrosternal joint (Option B): The first chondrosternal joint is also a primary cartilaginous joint, formed by hyaline cartilage between the first rib and the manubrium. It is rigid and non-movable, consistent with the characteristics of primary cartilaginous joints.

Costochondral joints (Option C): Costochondral joints, between ribs and their costal cartilages, are primary cartilaginous joints. They are united by hyaline cartilage, allowing stability but no significant movement. They serve as classic examples of synchondroses.

question_text: Which type of joint is present at the arrow mark joint shown in the x ray?

Explanation:

In the given X-ray of the bony pelvis, the marked joint is the pubic symphysis. It is an example of a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis).

question_text: A deep puncture wound in the palmar surface of the little finger near the proximal IP joint might introduce infection into which synovial cavity:
explanation:
The ulnar bursa is a synovial sheath covering the digital flexor tendons it covers the flexor tendons as they pass under the flexor retinaculum and terminates near the center of the palm for the second, third, and fourth fingers. However, the portion of the ulnar bursa which is concerned with the fifth finger does not terminate in the middle of the palm instead, it continues all the way into the insertion of the profundus tendon into the fifth digital phalanx. This means that a superficial cut on the palmar side of the fifth digit can introduce an infection into the ulnar bursa. The radial bursa is the other bursa associated with the flexor tendons it is a synovial sheath for flexor pollicis longus that extends to the point where this tendon inserts on the distal phalanx of the thumb. A superficial cut on the palmar side of the thumb might introduce an infection into the radial bursa. See Netter Plate 446 to get a good idea of these bursae

Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts on the pisiform, hamate, and the fifth metacarpal so, the bursa associated with this tendon would not be found near the digits. The fibrous digital sheath of the fingers covers the ulnar bursa and the flexor tendons these sheaths hold the tendons on the fingers. The intercarpal joint space is the space between the carpal bones.

question_text: Which of the following structures is unique to a synovial joint?
explanation:
The joint cavity, or synovial cavity, is the one structure that is unique to a synovial joint. This cavity is lined by a synovial membrane or articular cartilage and supported by a joint capsule or capsular ligament. The synovial membrane is made of vascular connective tissue which produces synovial fluid that fills the joint cavity. Accessory and collateral ligaments, bursae, and fibrocartilage may be found at synovial joints, but they are not unique to synovial joints.

Reference: Textbook of B d Chaurasia's handbook of General Anatomy, 4th Edition, Page number - 57

question_text: A worker doing repetitive lifting develops an inflammation in the tendon of origin of the extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle, commonly called "tennis elbow". The focal point of pain would most likely be near which palpable bony landmark?
explanation:
The extensor carpi radialis brevis muscle originates from the common extensor tendon off the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. So, an injury to this tendon would result in pain near the lateral epicondyle. Tennis elbow is due to the repetitive use of superficial extensor muscles of the forearm the pain is often felt at the lateral epicondyle and it radiates down the posterior surface of the forearm. None of the other bony landmarks are associated with the common extensor tendon, although the medial epicondyle is the origin of the common flexor tendon.

question_text: The point of insertion of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon to the index finger is on the:
explanation:
The flexor digitorum superficialis tendon inserts on the middle phalanx of fingers 2-5; the flexor digitorum profundus tendon inserts on the base of the distal phalanx of fingers 2-5. Both muscles flex the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, but flexor digitorum profundus is the only muscle that flexes the distal interphalangeal joints.

question_text: Which of the following muscle tendons does not insert into the dorsal digital expansion?
explanation:
Explanation:

Dorsal digital expansion (extensor expansion):

  • The central slip of extensor digitorum forms the middle portion.
  • The interossei and lumbrical tendons join its lateral margins, forming the wing tendons. (Options B & C)

question_text: In an attempt to commit suicide by slashing the ventral side of the wrist, the two tendons of the flexor digitorum superficialis located most superficially were completely severed. What movement would be affected?
option_a: Flexion of the MP and IP joints of the thumb
option_b: Flexion of the PIP joints of digits 2 and 5
option_c: Flexion of the PIP joints of digits 3 and 4
option_d: Flexion of the DIP joints of digits 2 and 5
explanation:
When cutting the ventral side of the wrist, the first tendons cut would be the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis. These tendons help flex the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, but not the distal interphalangeal joints. Flexor digitorum profundus (which has deeper tendons) is responsible for flexing the distal interphalangeal joints. To understand the next part of the question, look at Netter plate 443. The tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis are arranged in a packet with two superficial tendons and two deeper tendons. The tendons that go to fingers 3 and 4 are superficial, while the ones to finger 2 and 5 are underneath. So, the tendons to fingers 3 and 4 will be cut, impairing flexion of the proximal interphalangeal joints of digits 3 and 4.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Upper Limb Page number - 801

question_text: The marked number 1,2 & 6 make up what muscle group ?
explanation:
The three muscles acting on the thumb (APL, EPB, and EPL) are deep to the superficial extensors and emerge ("crop out") from a furrow in the lateral part of the forearm that divides the extensors. Because of this characteristic, they are referred to as outcropping muscles. The tendons of the APL and EPB bound the triangular anatomical snuff box laterally, and the tendon of the EPL bounds it medially. The snuff box is visible as a hollow on the lateral aspect of the wrist when the thumb is extended fully; this draws the APL, EPB, and EPL tendons up and produces a concavity between them. Observe that the: Radial artery lies on the floor of the snuff box. Radial styloid process can be palpated proximally and the base of the first metacarpal can be palpated distally in the snuff box. Scaphoid and trapezium can be felt in the floor of the snuff box between the radial styloid process and the first metacarpal.

question_text: Identify the tendon marked in the image
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The tendon marked in the image is the flexor carpi radialis.
  • Flexor carpi radialis is a long flexor located in the anterior compartment of the forearm.
  • It originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and runs toward the wrist.
  • Being a superficial muscle, its tendon becomes prominent when the wrist is flexed.

Muscles of Anterior Forearm:

  • The anterior compartment of the forearm contains the flexor muscles, which are organized into superficial and deep groups. Most of these muscles originate from the medial epicondyle of the humerus, also called the common flexor origin. Inflammation at this site is known as golfer’s elbow.
  • These muscles primarily cross the elbow and wrist joints, enabling flexion at these joints. Those that also cross the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints assist in flexing the fingers.
  • There are eight muscles in total in the anterior forearm: five superficial and three deep.

question_text: Pain may result from friction of the tendon of which muscle that passes deep to the anterior fibers of the long plantar ligament.
explanation:
Fibularis longus runs from the lateral side of the foot across the entire sole of the foot, traveling deep to the long plantar ligament. The friction between these two closely related structures may lead to discomfort. The tendon of tibialis posterior crosses behind the medial malleolus and enters the plantar surface of the foot on the medial side, inserting on navicular, the medial cuneiform, and metatarsals 2-4. The tendon of flexor digitorum longus travels posterior to the medial malleolus, and inserts on the bases of the distal phalanges of digits. The tendon of flexor hallucius longus also crosses behind the medial malleolus, travels under sustentaculum tali, and inserts on the base of the distal phalanx of the first toe. Finally, tibialis anterior does not really cross onto the plantar surface. It travels across the dorsum of the foot, and its tendon inserts on the medial surface of the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal.

question_text: Which of the following is an example of bipennate muscle?
explanation:
Explanation:

Peroneus longus is a classic example of a bipennate muscle, where muscle fibers are arranged obliquely on both sides of a central tendon, resembling a feather. This arrangement allows the muscle to generate greater force compared to parallel muscles. Bipennate architecture is typically seen in muscles requiring powerful contractions.

Types of Oblique Arrangements:

  • Triangular: e.g., Temporalis, Adductor Longus
  • Unipennate: e.g., Flexor Pollicis Longus, Extensor Digitorum Longus, Peroneus Tertius, Palmar Interossei.
  • Bipennate: e.g., Rectus Femoris, Dorsal Interossei, Peroneus Longus, Flexor Hallucis Longus
  • Multipennate: e.g., Subscapularis, Deltoid (Acromial Fibers)
  • Circumpennate: e.g., Tibialis Anterior

question_text: Which of the following statement is not correct regarding the marked tendon:
option_a: It connects the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles in the calf to an insertion point at the calcaneus
option_b: It is the strongest tendon in the body and allows people to push off while walking, running and jumping.
option_c: The Achilles tendon is a thick tendon located in the back of the leg.
option_d: Pain along the back of the Femur or in the hip are often the result of distinct problems
explanation:
Pain along the back of the ankle or in the heel are often the result of distinct problems along the course of the Achilles tendon or at its point of attachment to the heel of the foot. This type of pain may also be caused by retrocalcaneal bursitis, which is sometimes called Achilles tendon bursitis

The Achilles tendon is a thick tendon located in the back of the leg. It connects the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles in the calf to an insertion point at the calcaneus (heel bone). It is the strongest tendon in the body and allows people to push off while walking, running and jumping.

Achilles injuries can occur in several places, but the most common area is at the muscle-tendon junction - the area where the calf muscles join with the tendon. Injuries in this area often heal on their own. This junction has a smaller blood supply than does the muscular area of the leg, however.

This makes the healing process slower than it is in many other leg injuries.

question_text: Which joint would be subject to synovitis (inflammation of the synovial membrane)?
explanation:
This question is asking you to pick what joint, of the joints listed, is the synovial joint. And the only one which fits the bill is the metacarpophalangeal joint, which is a condyloid synovial joint, meaning that it can move in a sagittal and coronal plane. Condyloid joints permit flexion and extension, abduction and adduction, and circumduction. Beyond the synovial membrane, synovial joints have a variety of important characteristics, including: hyaline cartilage to cover the weight bearing surface of the joint, a joint capsule made of accessory ligaments to reinforce the synovial membrane, and accessory structures (such as accessory ligaments, articular discs or menisci, muscles and tendons, and subsynovial fat).

question_text: A 50 years old traffic policeman presents to hospital with pain on the sole of foot near heel. The pain is worse with the first few steps in morning or after periods of rest. On examination doctor observed tenderness at the medial aspect of the heel. There is no history of trauma. What is the most likely diagnosis for patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Plantar fasciitis

  • Inflammation of plantar aponeurosis.
  • Occurs in individuals who do a great deal of standing and walking.
  • It causes pain and tenderness in the sole of the foot, especially underneath the heel during standing.

Plantar aponeurosis:

  • Triangular in shape
  • Represent distal part of plantaris.
  • Apex attached to medial tubercle of calcaneum
  • Base divided into 5 processes which further split to superficial and deep slip
  • Superficial slip is attached to dermis of skin and deep slip embrace the flexor tendons
  • It fixes the skin of sole and protects the deeper structure.
  • It helps in maintaining the longitudinal arches of the foot.

Tarsal tunnel syndrome: It is due to a compression of tibial nerve between the flexor retinaculum and calcaneum. Symptoms includes tingling and numbness in sole of foot.

Achilles tendinitis: It is a inflammation of Achilles tendon due to increase physical activity mostly seen in athletes. Symptoms includes pain and tenderness around the ankle.

Stress fracture: Mostly affects the metatarsal due to sudden increase in sports activity.

Key Takeaways:

Heel pain that is most severe with the first steps in the morning or after rest is the classic finding for Plantar fasciitis.

Moderate

question_text: What muscle tendon is enclosed within its own synovial sheath in the carpal canal?

question_text: In lymphatic drainage of the breast, the major portion (about 75%) enters eventually into which group of nodes?

question_text: Which of the following arrangements correctly represents the contents of the cubital fossa from medial to lateral side?

Explanation:

The contents of the cubital fossa from medial to lateral follow the sequence MBBR:

  • Brachial artery
  • Biceps tendon

Cubital fossa:

  • A triangular depression located anterior to the elbow joint.

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the anatomy of the breast?
option_a: The superior medial quadrant has more tissue
option_c: The axillary tail of Spence crosses the anterior axillary fold
option_d: The nipple is located at the level of the fourth intercostal space in most women
explanation:
Explanation:

The axillary tail of Spence is an extension of breast tissue that projects from the upper outer quadrant of the breast into the axilla, passing over the anterior axillary fold. This tail contains a significant portion of glandular tissue and is clinically important during breast examinations.


Breast and Mammary Glands:

Breast: The breast contains mammary glands located within the superficial fascia. It extends vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib along the midclavicular line and horizontally from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line at the level of the 4th rib.

Suspensory Ligaments of Cooper: These ligaments anchor the breast tissue (parenchyma) to the overlying skin and the underlying pectoral fascia. In cases of malignancy, tumor invasion along these ligaments can cause skin dimpling.

Nipple: The nipple's position varies among adult women, influenced by breast size and shape. In nulliparous women, it is typically located at the level of the 4th intercostal space (Option D ruled out). The nipple is pierced by 15-20 lactiferous ducts through which milk is secreted.

Areola: This is the pigmented ring of skin surrounding the nipple.

Mammary Gland: The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland. The axillary tail of Spence is a tail-like extension of breast tissue that projects from the upper outer quadrant into the axilla.

Retromammary Space: This space contains loose connective tissue situated between the base of the breast gland and the deep fascia covering the mammary bed.

The breast is composed of 15-20 lobes of glandular tissue, separated by fibrous septa radiating outward from the nipple (Option B ruled out). Each lobe drains through a lactiferous duct, which widens to form a lactiferous sinus near the nipple.

Explanation of other options:

The superior medial quadrant has more tissue (Option A): The superior lateral quadrant of the breast contains more glandular tissue than the superior medial quadrant. This increased tissue volume is due to the axillary tail of Spence, which carries a substantial portion of the glandular elements into the axilla.

question_text: A 42-year-old man presented with swelling due to a collection of blood around the eyes after sustaining a head injury. Which structural attachment is the cause of this condition?

The scalp consists of five distinct layers:

question_text: A 46-year-old woman presents with a noticeable change in the size and appearance of her left nipple. On examination, the doctor finds a painless, hard lump in the breast that is fixed to the underlying tissues and immobile. Additional findings include nipple retraction, peau d'orange appearance of the skin, and enlarged axillary lymph nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a painless hard mass, fixation to deeper structures, nipple retraction, skin dimpling (peau d'orange), and axillary lymphadenopathy is characteristic of breast carcinoma.

These features indicate infiltration of surrounding ligaments, ducts, and lymphatic channels.

Carcinoma of breast:

  • Most common malignancy in females.
  • Typically arises from the epithelial lining of the lactiferous ducts (invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type).

Common clinical features:

  • Painless hard lump: due to malignant proliferation.
  • Fixation of the breast mass: caused by tumor infiltration into suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments, making the breast immobile.
  • Skin retraction: infiltration and tethering of Cooper's ligaments.
  • Nipple retraction: fibrosis and shortening of lactiferous ducts.
  • Peau d'orange appearance: obstruction of superficial lymphatics, causing edema while hair follicles remain anchored, giving an orange-skin appearance.
  • Enlarged axillary lymph nodes: common pathway of lymphatic spread.

Fibroadenoma (Option A): Benign mobile breast lump; smooth, non-fixed, and typically painless. Does not cause nipple retraction or peau d'orange.

Breast abscess (Option B): Painful, warm, red swelling often with fever; usually associated with lactation.

Galactocoele (Option C): Milk-filled cyst seen during or after lactation; soft, cystic, and non-adherent.

question_text: All of the following skin receptors are present in the dermis of the skin, EXCEPT:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The Merkel's corpuscle (Option A) is located in the stratum basale of the epidermis, making it the only receptor among the options that is not found in the dermis.
    • Merkel endings are thought to be slow-adapting mechanoreceptors, responsive to sustained pressure and sensitive to the edges of applied objects.
  • In contrast, Meissner's corpuscle, Pacinian corpuscle, and Ruffini's corpuscle are all located in the dermis and play crucial roles in sensation:

  • Meissner's corpuscle (Option B): Meissner's corpuscles (Wagner-Meissner corpuscles; tactile corpuscle-like bodies) are found in the dermal papillae of all parts of the hand and foot, the anterior aspect of the forearm, the lips, palpebral conjunctiva and mucous membrane of the apical part of the tongue.
    • Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors, sensitive to shape and textural changes in exploratory and discriminatory touch.
  • Pacinian corpuscle (Option C): Located in the dermis, sensitive to deep pressure and vibration.
    • Pacinian corpuscles are situated subcutaneously in the palmar and plantar aspects of the hand and foot and their digits, the external genitalia, arm, neck, nipple, periosteal and interosseous membranes, and near joints and within the mesenteries.
  • Ruffini's corpuscle (Option D): They are found in the dermis of thin, hairy skin, where they function as dermal stretch receptors and are responsive to maintained stresses in dermal collagen.

Key Takeaways:

  • Merkel's corpuscle is located in the epidermis, distinguishing it from other skin receptors present in the dermis.
  • The skin contains both encapsulated and non-encapsulated receptors, enabling it to respond to various sensory stimuli effectively.
